newsitem.title: UK: UK insurers get court injunction against ad report.
newsitem.headline: UK insurers get court injunction against ad report.

text.p: A British advertising watchdog said on Thursday it had been prevented by a court injunction from publishing a report mentioning a complaint about an insurance group's advertising.

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), a self-regulatory body that oversees print advertising, said the injunction, which was issued on August 8, covered a judgment by the ASA that was scheduled for publication this week, about Direct Line insurance group.

It was one of the reports the ASA publishes every month that describes complaints by the public about various advertising and that explains whether the ASA has decided to uphold any of the complaints.

Campaign and Marketing Week, Britain's two main weekly magazines on the advertising industry, reported on Thursday that Direct Line had successfully sought an injunction from the High Court in London.
Direct Line, which is owned by the Royal Bank of Scotland, pioneered the business of selling insurance over the telephone in Britain.
The magazines said Direct Line sought the injunction because the ASA, after receiving one or more complaints from the public about an ad for the insurance group, had decided to ban the ad.
The ASA, when asked by Reuters about the magazine reports, declined to give details about the case, but confirmed the High Court issued the injunction after being asked to do so by Direct Line.
A spokesman said the ASA's monthly report had subsequently been revised by taking out any reference to the Direct Line case and the revised report would be released on August 20.
The vast majority of advertisers in Britain whose ads get banned by the ASA agree to follow the authority's judgment and it is unusual for advertisers to take the ASA to court.
But some advertisers and advertising executives have recently questioned whether the ASA, which has no statutory enforcement power, had sufficient clout to police the advertising industry.
The ASA spokesman, when asked, said he was not worried the case would threaten the ASA's position.

"We are not worried about the effect of this case on the ASA's authority. It's not the first time that an injunction has been sought and other companies would need to have convincing grounds on which to seek another injunction," he said.
Campaign said the ad in question was about a service offered by Direct Line called an Instant Access Savings account.
